the open-source community.

## Why it exists {#why-it-exists}

Physics is best understood by building, experimenting, and verifying results
yourself. A textbook states a result; here you construct it as a program,
test it against measurements or against a second method, and, where it can be
done, prove it. Doing all three on one problem shows what each kind of
evidence can and cannot establish.

### Why open source {#why-open-source}

The code behind every simulation, figure, and proof is openly available for
anyone to explore, reproduce, and improve. The project is freely accessible
without registration or tracking.

## Who it is for {#who-it-is-for}

Readers who have undergraduate physics (classical mechanics, calculus, linear
algebra) and solid programming skills: students who want to see a result
computed rather than asserted, researchers who want to check that it
reproduces, and teachers who want material they can run in class. Lessons
state their prerequisites and link out instead of repeating them. Teaching
with a lesson? The [For educators](educators.qmd) page lists the instructor
packs.

## What makes it different {#what-this-site-is}

The lessons are organised in two parts, not as one ladder from easy to hard.
Computational and experimental physics has eight courses:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from pbc.authoring.path import COURSES, METHOD_PATHS

print("\n".join(f"- {course.title}" for course in COURSES))
print()
print(
    "Physics with language models and AI agents has four method paths, each a"
    " sequence of lessons that may draw on any of the courses:"
)
print()
print("\n".join(f"- {title}" for _, title in METHOD_PATHS))
```

Every lesson belongs to one course and teaches by three activities:
**construct** the physics as a program you can run, **investigate** it with
simulations, with real measurements, and with experiments that an AI agent
helps to run, and **verify** the result by tests, by independent checks, or
by a proof in Lean that a machine checks. Each lesson names the lessons it
builds on, so you can read a course from its start, follow one method across
courses, or begin with any lesson whose prerequisites you have. The
[Course Atlas](path/index.qmd) shows every course, path, and lesson.

## How the results are checked {#how-the-site-is-built}

- Code shown in a lesson is code the build ran. Figures and numbers are the
  output of that code, regenerated on every build.
- Proofs are compiled by Lean on every change. A lesson whose code fails or
  whose proof does not compile cannot be published.
- A statement that could be read as a scientific result is marked as a claim
  with its type and the evidence behind it; a claim without evidence stops
  the build. The [Evidence map](evidence.qmd) lists every claim.
- Every lesson ends with the commands that reproduce it on your own
  computer; [Run the code](reproduce.qmd) says what to install.
- Equations are MathML. Text, code, equations, and figures are readable with
  JavaScript turned off. The site is static files. It has no accounts, sets
  no cookies, runs no analytics, and loads nothing from other websites.

The [rendering check](rendering-check.qmd) page shows sample equations, code,
and a figure produced by this pipeline.

## How to contribute

To correct a mistake, propose a change, suggest a dataset, or propose a lesson,

## How to cite

The repository has a `CITATION.cff` file in the
[Citation File Format](https://citation-file-format.github.io/). GitHub reads
it and offers "Cite this repository". It names the authors, the project
address, the repository, and the licences. It has no DOI: none exists until
the project has a release policy. A suitable citation is "Physics by
Construction", with a link to the page you used.
